Review: The protocol is substantially more implementable and interpretable than a design based on the supplied aggregate export alone. It defines a clear primary coupling contrast, separates calibration from confirmation, uses randomized blocked runs, and addresses synchronization, reset failures, drive delivery, censoring, and run-level uncertainty. Its feasibility nevertheless depends on access to the functioning 111-unit array, synchronized unit-level measurements, and enough apparatus time for independent resets and repeated trials. The provided data do not establish that these resources or the required signal quality are available.

Feedback: Before committing to the confirmatory study, use the calibration pilot to demonstrate that coupling settings produce distinct coarsening rates while maintaining stable operation and comparable drive delivery and disorder. Confirm that the subharmonic can be resolved in the planned window length and that the null procedure controls false detections across the full onset search. Then use pilot variance, reset success, and observed throughput to set a realistic run count and observation duration; the protocol’s precision target and maximum run count should be achievable within available apparatus time. One methodological point needs tightening: specify how the restricted mean onset-time contrast will be estimated when runs are censored, and how the onset-time analysis will handle failures or missing windows that may be informative. The staged drive control is a useful comparison but adds material time and should follow only after the primary study’s resource needs are secured. The optional disorder condition should remain outside the confirmatory scope unless separately powered and preregistered.

Rating (1-5): 3. The design is feasible in principle, but its practical success is conditional on specialized apparatus access, reliable resets and synchronization, and sufficient independent-run throughput. The supplied aggregate measurements cannot establish these prerequisites or support a sample-size estimate.
